analysis.one_liner: Repeals upcoming air pollution limits for cars and trucks, freezing emissions standards at 1995 levels.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by Rep. Tom DeLay with one cosponsor, was referred to committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Clean Air Act so that every vehicle made after model year 1995, in every category, only had to meet the 1995 emissions standard. It would repeal tougher upcoming limits on nitrogen oxide pollution from heavy-duty trucks after 1997, repeal tighter standards for light-duty trucks after 1995, and cancel a required study of whether cars need further emission cuts. In practice, it would lock in the pollution rules already in place and erase the planned next steps.
analysis.who_benefits: Vehicle manufacturers, especially heavy-duty truck makers, would avoid the cost of meeting stricter nitrogen oxide limits that had not yet taken effect. Fleets and buyers of new trucks might see lower upfront vehicle costs.

how_it_helps.text: It freezes the emissions standard for all motor vehicles manufactured after model year 1995 at the standard applicable in that model year, so no vehicle category faces tighter future limits.
It repeals the nitrogen oxide emissions standards for heavy-duty trucks for model years after 1997, before they could take effect.
It repeals specified upcoming emissions standards for light-duty trucks after model year 1995 and the required study on whether further reductions from light-duty vehicles are necessary.

analysis.who_pays: People who live with the resulting air pollution would bear the cost, since the repealed standards targeted nitrogen oxides, a contributor to smog and respiratory health problems. The bill shifts compliance costs away from manufacturers and onto air quality.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone breathing the resulting air pollution

drawbacks.text: Repealing the upcoming nitrogen oxide standards for heavy-duty trucks and tighter light-duty truck standards would allow more smog-forming pollution than the existing Clean Air Act trajectory, with the health burden falling on the public rather than on vehicle buyers' upfront prices.

Even supporters of regulatory relief generally acknowledge that delaying cleaner vehicle technology pushes compliance costs into the future rather than eliminating them, since air quality rules would eventually have to be revisited.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades lower compliance costs for vehicle makers against higher smog-forming emissions for the public. Because it repeals standards before they take effect and cancels the study meant to guide future decisions, its benefit is concentrated on manufacturers while its costs are diffuse and fall on public health.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Commerce Committee, then to its Health and Environment Subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended without ever reaching the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom DeLay introduced the bill on January 11, 1995, to repeal Clean Air Act emissions standards for motor vehicles that had not yet taken effect.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce, which held no further action on it.
On February 6, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where it remained for the rest of the 104th Congress.
The bill drew a single cosponsor and never received a committee vote or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people came out ahead in the narrow sense that the tighter truck emissions standards the bill targeted were not repealed. Vehicle manufacturers did not get the regulatory relief they would have gained, since the bill died in subcommittee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyone affected by the unrepealed air standards

for.name: Rep. Tom DeLay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal not-yet-effective motor vehicle emissions standards.

against.name: House Committee on Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out or scheduled action on it.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health and Environment
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 6, 1995, and took no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes on the bill; its sponsorship was entirely Republican (the sponsor plus one Republican cosponsor), so no partisan pattern beyond that can be established.

industries.note: The bill would repeal the nitrogen oxide standards for heavy-duty trucks for model years after 1997, sparing them compliance costs before the rules took effect. The cost would be higher smog-forming emissions for the public.

The bill would freeze all post-1995 vehicles at the 1995 emissions standard and repeal tighter light-duty truck standards, easing regulatory pressure. Ordinary people would absorb the air quality cost.
